item.title: Elon Musk settles fraud lawsuits over his $1 million giveaways to 2024 voters
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk attends the Golden Age of American Innovation Summit at the Institute of Peace on October 08, 2026 in Washington, DC. - Win McNamee/Getty Images Tech billionaire and Republican megadonor Elon Musk on Thursday settled the two remaining lawsuits stemming from his $1 million giveaways to voters during the 2024 election, according to court filings, bringing a two-year legal saga to an end. During the final stretch of the 2024 presidential race, Musk’s super PAC started a daily $1 million giveaway to registered voters in battleground states, while Musk was urging voters to support Donald Trump. After the election, voters in a handful of battleground states filed proposed class-action civil fraud lawsuits against Musk and his political group, America PAC, which both deny wrongdoing. The voters claimed Musk duped them into believing that they’d have a fair shot at the money if they signed up for the sweepstakes — which included turning over their private data to his political organization. Musk had publicly stated that the payouts would be given away “randomly” to registered voters. But his lawyers later conceded in court that winners were “not chosen by chance” but rather were picked based on whether they would be a strong spokesperson for the pro-Trump super PAC. In court filings from the two separate cases on Thursday, lawyers for Musk and for the voters said they had settled the litigation. The filings did not describe the terms of the settlements. CNN has requested comment from Musk spokesman and the lawyers representing the voters who sued him for comment. This year, Musk has reprised his role as a Republican megadonor — with at least $276 million in donations to GOP candidates for the midterm elections. He has also continued to be one of the leading promoters of election-related disinformation, as he was in 2024 . The Justice Department warned Musk back in 2024 that the million-dollar giveaways could violate longstanding federal laws against vote-buying. The Philadelphia District Attorney filed a lawsuit to shut down the sweepstakes while it was still happening, but a state judge ruled on the eve of Election Day that it could proceed. The bipartisan Wisconsin Election Commission concluded earlier this year that Musk likely broke state law with similar cash giveaways in a 2025 state judicial race. But prosecutors declined to bring charges because, they said, the evidence was too weak to secure a bribery conviction. This story has been updated with additional information. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/15/politics/elon-musk-settles-lawsuits-one-million-dollars-giveaways

item.title: Trump administration sued over collection of sensitive voter data from 47 states
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Trump administration is being sued over its efforts to collect and analyze sensitive voter data from across the country. The complaint, filed in federal court in Washington, D.C., on Thursday, alleges the Department of Homeland Security has obtained voter files from at least 47 states and handled the data in a way that violates federal law. DHS' secretive probe of the voter data, which includes a policy to combine it with commercial datasets, ignores federal safeguards and the privacy rights of millions of Americans, the lawsuit says. The case was brought by the League of Women Voters, the Electronic Privacy Information Center and the League of United Latin American Citizens and is the latest legal challenge to President Donald Trump's efforts to combat noncitizen voting. State Department Considers Sharing Passport Records For Voter Citizenship Checks The Trump administration is being sued over its efforts to collect and analyze sensitive voter data from across the country. The president has purported repeatedly argued that noncitizen voting poses a serious threat to election integrity, although studies and prosecutions have found documented instances of noncitizens casting ballots to be rare. Read On The Fox News App The administration has repeatedly sought a greater federal role in voter eligibility and election administration, areas traditionally overseen primarily by states under the Constitution and federal law. Federal courts have repeatedly rejected administration efforts to compel states to turn over voter information. The new lawsuit alleges the administration has obtained and processed voter records from at least 47 states, even though officials in 30 states have previously refused federal demands to turn over voter information. The complaint urges the court to declare the administration's collection of voter data illegal, block DHS' policy and order the agency to delete and stop using the voter information it has already obtained. The lawsuit comes less than three weeks before Election Day, and the administration continues to pressure states, alleging they are not doing enough to purge noncitizens from their voter rolls. Trump Scores Supreme Court Win In Election Integrity Fight As States Gain New Voter Roll Tool The president has repeatedly argued that noncitizen voting poses a serious threat to election integrity, although documented instances of noncitizens casting ballots are rare. The Justice Department asked a judge to block the state from counting mail-in ballots from those individuals unless their eligibility can be confirmed. The California secretary of state's office said it was given only 48 hours to review roughly 20,000 names and said the federal government had not provided the underlying evidence or methodology supporting its claims. The Justice Department's lawsuit, however, says U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services conducted a "multiagency and multilevel review" and determined with "high confidence" that roughly 20,000 people on California's voter rolls were likely noncitizens. DHS did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. The Associated Press contributed to this report. item.title: Trump calls Ukraine's renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries 'a disgrace'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Plumes of smoke rise from an oil refinery after a Ukrainian drone strike in Moscow on 20 September. Photograph: Reuters Donald Trump has called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” and criticised Volodymyr ⁠Zelenskyy after an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold. Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries ⁠after Zelenskyy said Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire unilaterally declared by Trump on Sunday, having briefly halted its attacks to demonstrate its readiness for peace talks. Russia had continued its strikes on Ukrainian power plants. Related: Russia and Ukraine trade strikes as Trump ‘energy ceasefire’ collapses In an interview with Newsmax aired on Thursday, the US president said: “All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that’s a disgrace. “There are a lot ‌of targets you can ‌hit, but when you shoot at diesel refineries where you make, you know, ‌diesel oil, and we need that, and the world needs that, then he’s not doing a good service for the world.” Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since Trump announced an easing sanctions on Russia in exchange for Moscow releasing large amounts of diesel on to global markets. Zelenskyy criticised the agreement, which was widely interpreted as an attempt to curb high fuel prices before the US midterm elections, saying it would allow Russia to press on with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that began more than four and a half years ago. US efforts under Trump to end the war have made no progress. Trump repeated to Newsmax his views of the two leaders involved in the conflict. “I’m not a big fan of Zelenskyy,” Trump said. “I think they actually both would like to see it ⁠end, but I think I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult ​to deal with ​than Putin.” Arriving in Brussels to meet EU leaders on Friday, Zelenskyy did not comment on Trump’s latest remarks. He said he was “so thankful that we have such huge support from the EU” and its leaders, whom he described as “real leaders”. He went on to say that Ukraine wanted to end the war as quickly as possible, but “we don’t see now signals from [the] Russian side that they are ready for this”. Kyiv’s relationship with Washington was strained further this week when Ukraine said Starlink services had been restricted , in effect hobbling Ukrainian drone strike missions and crucial air defences with a flick of the switch. During a visit to London this week, the Ukrainian president said the sudden restriction of Starlink had left him feeling personally betrayed by Trump and lamented losing a partner. Related: Russia and Ukraine trade strikes as Trump ‘energy ceasefire’ collapses The British defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said on Thursday that his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, had assured him in a face-to-face meeting that the vital satellite communications system had been restored. In an interview with the BBC, he said it was unclear what had caused the disruption, but added: “This is not the first time we’ve seen a falling out between Washington and Kyiv.” Amid growing doubts about long-term US commitment to Ukraine, European leaders declared their support for Zelenskyy. Standing alongside the Ukrainian leader in Brussels, the European Council president, António Costa, said Ukraine could “count on us not only to support you in war” but also in the path to negotiating EU membership. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU had supported Trump’s energy ceasefire, “but we have seen that Russia did not respect it, not a single minute” and instead had escalated its attacks. She said the EU intended to increase pressure on Russia, promising a 22nd round of sanctions, adding: “We will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops the war.” The promise of further European sanctions against Russia comes weeks after the EU lifted sanctions against two prominent Russian oligarchs at the request of France and Luxembourg. After meeting Zelenskyy, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, said it was “crucial” that Ukraine received “all the means necessary to protect itself”. The Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, posted online: “I can reassure you, dear Ukrainian friends and President Zelenskyy: YOU ARE NOT ALONE.” As Zelenskyy met Macron in Brussels, he said that the Kremlin had “launched yet another vile drone strike on Ukrainian energy infrastructure” in the city of Lutsk, which caused blackouts. The Kremlin, meanwhile, accused Ukraine of derailing US peace efforts by resuming its strikes on refineries. item.title: The midterm polls are predicting a blue wave. Can they be trusted?
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Anyone who's followed American politics over the past decade or so has learned to look at political polls with a healthy dose of skepticism. Some of the most important recent elections have featured substantial polling errors that left many Americans baffled when things turned out differently than they expected. As we head into a pivotal midterm election, the polls are generally telling the same story. Forecasts point to the possibility of a blue wave that will sweep across the country, likely allowing Democrats to flip control of the House of Representatives and giving them a chance of gaining a majority in the Senate as well. Is that story true, though? We won't know for certain until after the actual votes are counted, but there is evidence that can give us a slightly better sense of what the polls are seeing, what they might be missing and how well other political trends match the picture that the polls are painting. What the polls say In a midterm election, there are three types of polls to watch if you want a sense of where things stand in the battle for control of Congress. The first tracks the approval rating of someone who isn't even on the ballot in November: the president of the United States. Historically speaking, a president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his first two years in office. (The average number lost since World War II? Twenty-six .) Sometimes, the backlash is so pervasive that the president's party loses seats across a wide range of competitive districts — a phenomenon known as a "wave" election. Yahoo Knowing how Americans feel about the president's job performance is helpful because they tend to channel those feelings into their votes for the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives. Right now, 60% of Americans, on average, disapprove of how President Trump is handling his job, according to the data journalists at Silver Bulletin ; 38% approve. That puts the president's net disapproval rating at about 22 percentage points. Trump is earning even lower marks on voters' top issue this year: the cost of living . Shortly after he returned to office, roughly equal numbers of Americans approved and disapproved of how the president was handling inflation. But today — as tariffs and the Iran war help drive prices up — 71% disapprove and 25% approve . That's a 46-point gap. The second type of poll to pay attention to is what's known (at least among politics nerds) as the "generic ballot," which typically asks something along the lines of: If an election for U.S. Congress were held today, which party's candidate would you vote for in your district? This is our best measure of how partisan sentiment is shaping up across all 435 U.S. House contests. At the moment, Democrats have a lead on the generic ballot — nearly 9 percentage points , on average — and Republican support has been trending downward since September. To put that in perspective, Democrats were leading by an average of 7 points on the generic ballot at this point in 2018, with Trump as president and Republican majorities in the House and Senate. Three weeks later, Democrats picked up 41 seats and flipped the House. (This year, Democrats need to net only three seats to win control of that chamber.) The third and final type of polling that matters in a congressional midterm cycle is state surveys of key Senate contests. Here's where the data gets a little trickier. In recent weeks, the preponderance of polling has shown Democrats widening their leads in competitive states where they're defending seats they already hold ( Georgia , Minnesota , New Hampshire , Michigan ) while also gaining ground in red states where they're trying to flip a Republican-held seat ( Alaska , Iowa , Texas , Kansas , Ohio ). Some Republicans are arguing that this red-state Senate polling could be inaccurate — and pointing to past polling "misses" to make their case. How badly have polls missed in the past? It's important to note that polling errors should be expected in any race. Polling is an inexact science. No matter how sophisticated a pollster's process is, it invariably includes assumptions, adjustments and extrapolations that leave a lot of room for error. That uncertainty has been a feature of election polling throughout its history. Those misses are less impactful in years where the variance in polls balances out. If they underestimate the Republicans' strength in some races while overselling the GOP in others, you end up with polling that generally reflects the actual results in the aggregate. The problem over the past decade is that, in multiple elections, the polls have mostly missed in the same direction. Trump's win over Hillary Clinton in 2016 came as such a surprise because polls had systematically underestimated his support. When it came to the national popular vote , the polls were relatively accurate. The big misses came in the swing states that decided the election. Heading into Election Day, polls showed Clinton ahead — sometimes by a large margin — in five states that Trump ended up winning. The 2016 election sparked a reckoning within the polling world. The major polling firms realized that something had made them underestimate the size of Trump's voting coalition. They spent years making changes to how they collect and interpret data to fix that clear blind spot. Donald Trump addresses supporters during a campaign rally in Denver, Colo., on Nov. 5, 2016. JASON CONNOLLY via Getty Images Things looked more promising after the 2018 midterms. The polls were reasonably accurate. When they did miss, they missed in both directions, meaning the polls weren't systematically biased against either party. Then came 2020. Even though the polls accurately predicted Joe Biden would win, they underestimated Republicans' support by even more than they had four years earlier. Trump performed nearly 3 percentage points better than expected in the national popular vote and outperformed polls in individual states by more than 4 points. The miss was even bigger in Senate and gubernatorial races. The polls bounced back in 2022, when they were more accurate than in any election in recent history, before once again underestimating Republicans in 2024 — though by a smaller margin than in either 2016 or 2020. The pattern over the past decade has been that polls have tended to be biased against Republicans when Trump is on the ballot and reasonably on point when he's not. While that could be considered reason for optimism among Democrats, five election cycles is hardly a definitive sample. Why the polls might be wrong A lot of explanations have been put forward to try to understand the polling misses in recent presidential elections. The most commonly cited is the belief that MAGA Republicans, due to their general lack of trust in mainstream institutions, are less likely to pick up the phone when a polling firm calls than members of other political groups. That phenomenon, which pollsters call "nonresponse bias," can skew survey samples and make the share of Republican voters appear smaller than it really is. "The polling is wrong. ... Republicans don't want to respond to polls anymore," House Speaker Mike Johnson told Fox News on Tuesday. Johnson and other Republicans have pointed to some surprising survey results on the Senate side to bolster their argument that polls might be missing GOP voters. That includes Democratic leads and strong showings by independents in Senate races in deep red states like Iowa , Kansas and Nebraska . For those polls to be accurate, voter sentiment would have had to have swung as much as 23 points in Democrats' direction since the last midterm Senate contests in those states. One pollster recently described GOP voters' nonresponse in a poll they conducted in Iowa as a "canary in the cornfields" for a potentially widespread undercounting of Republican support in the state. Polling firms try to account for nonresponse bias by adjusting their results to give less weight to people from groups who are overrepresented in their samples, but doing so means making a lot of assumptions about the nature of a constantly evolving electorate. It's possible that the adjustments they're making this year aren't enough to accurately reflect voters' sentiments. On top of gauging how people will vote, there's also the challenge of determining who will vote. Polls often include results for "likely" voters — voters who are expected to cast a ballot — but deciding who should fit into that category involves its own assumptions that can be wrong. Earlier this month, the polling firm YouGov released a survey showing Democrats up 16 points nationally with likely voters, a gap that YouGov itself described as "hard-to-believe." While the major recent polling errors have been in presidential election years, data compiled by Republican pollster Patrick Ruffini suggests that the polls have also had some noteworthy misses in midterm cycles as well. "Nationally, the polls were pretty good, but red state polls were too blue and blue state polls too red," he wrote on X . If Ruffini's analysis is accurate, that could mean that Democrats' chances of flipping Senate seats in states like Texas, Iowa and Ohio aren't nearly as strong as they appear to be. Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico of Texas speaks at a rally on July 13, 2026. AP Photo/Brenda Bazán Republicans also have more room for error in the House this year thanks to redistricting. The GOP's sweeping campaign to redraw congressional maps in red states gave them up to nine new safe House seats. Democrats tried to even the score by doing their own gerrymandering. But when the dust settled, Republicans still came out ahead. That said, Republicans might still struggle to keep their majority in the House even if the polls are off by a significant margin. On the other hand, when it comes to the Senate, the polls would only need to be off by a few points in a handful of key states for the GOP to maintain control over the chamber. Why the polls might be right Polling errors are commonplace; they happen in most elections. But they tend to be random and to change directions from one cycle to another . The argument that skeptics are making this time around is that there is something fundamentally different about the Trump era — something that systematically skews all poll results involving Trump. This has been true, to a degree, in each of the three presidential contests that Trump himself has competed in. There, the final average of polls conducted before Election Day underestimated Republicans' performance in the popular vote by an average of 3.8 percentage points, according to data journalist Nate Silver . But there has been no systematic polling bias toward Democrats in Trump-era elections when Trump himself was not on the ballot . In fact, the polls since 2016 have overestimated Republican support in midterm elections (by an average of 0.2%) and off-year, special and runoff elections (by an average of 1.3%), according to Silver . One possible explanation for this dynamic is that "the midterm electorate skews toward politically engaged voters who are more trusting of institutions and more likely to have answered polls," as the Atlantic recently put it . To be significantly wrong in 2026, the polls would have to be wrong in ways they weren't in 2022 and 2018. There are other reasons to believe the polls could be right as well. While there are signs that rural Republicans are not responding to pollsters in certain states , that doesn't necessarily mean that those voters are secretly planning to show up and surprise everyone on Election Day. Instead, experts say that it might mean the opposite: that they don't want to answer questions about politics because they are not particularly enthusiastic about voting this year. Pollsters aren't seeing this "rural nonresponse" effect everywhere , either. The Hidalgo County Republican Party Headquarters on Sept. 16, 2026, in McAllen, Texas. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson The parties are also behaving as if the polls are accurate. Republicans' spending patterns show that they are "pour[ing] money into dozens of U.S. House races previously considered 'safe,'" Reuters recently reported . Democrats are also campaigning hard in parts of the country that would typically be out of their reach. Meanwhile, "some top congressional Republicans have privately concluded that it is likely impossible for them to keep control of the House of Representatives in the midterm elections," according to Politico . On the Senate side, the major GOP campaign groups have reportedly cut back on spending in North Carolina and Georgia, a sign that they may be losing faith in winning those races, and rerouted the money to defend a historically safe seat in Kansas. None of this guarantees that the polls are right. They could be rife with the same errors that have plagued them in recent elections, or have new blind spots that won't become clear until later. However, the polls currently reflect what you might expect to see in a political environment in which historical precedent suggests the party in power will struggle, the president's approval rating is low, and the parties are battling it out in what are normally deep red parts of the country. We'll find out just how accurate the polls really are on Nov. 3. item.title: Ousted general warned of missile defense shortage before Iran war
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Washington — In late December, two months before the U.S. war with Iran began, Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George warned that his service was critically short on missile defense munitions and that the shortage would last another five years, according to multiple U.S. officials familiar with the matter. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ousted George in April, as the Iran war was underway. George's risk analysis appeared in the Pentagon's Global Force Management Allocation Plan, a defense secretary-approved annual order determining where troops and weapons will be allocated across the globe, according to the U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News. He warned that the stockpile of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense batteries and Patriot missiles would continue to be strategically low until 2030. His assessment was written for the Defense Department's plan for fiscal year 2027 and before the outbreak of the U.S.-Israel-led war with Iran, now in its seventh month. U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News under condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly said his assessment stemmed from the transfer of Patriots to Ukraine after Russia's invasion in 2022, the expenditure of munitions to defend Israel, and the reduced capacity of the defense industrial base. CBS News is withholding the exact percentage figures conveyed by U.S. officials because of security concerns, and George declined to comment. U.S. officials say that while the U.S. possesses a significant stockpile of some offensive munitions, like the Joint Direct Attack Munition and Small Diameter Bombs, missile defense munitions used in Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD, batteries, and Patriot missile systems are at low strategic-risk levels. The THAAD system is one of the U.S. military's most advanced missile defense systems, designed to intercept and destroy incoming ballistic missiles during the final phase of their flight, either inside or just outside Earth's atmosphere. The Army has eight THAAD batteries. Each battery consists of 90 soldiers who operate six truck-mounted launchers, with each truck possessing eight launchers. A full battery controls 48 interceptors, according to a 2025 report from the nonpartisan Congressional Research Service. The Patriot air-defense system is designed to protect military installations, troops and other critical infrastructure from incoming ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as hostile aircraft. It can engage a broader range of aerial threats at lower altitudes than a THAAD battery, but when used together, they provide even more effective overlapping layers of defense against missile attacks. The Patriot munition at a critical low is the Patriot Advanced Capability-3, or PAC-3, a high-velocity surface-to-air interceptor designed to destroy incoming tactical ballistic missiles and cruise missiles by ramming into them. PAC-3s can also bring down enemy aircraft, according to U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News. "Those are the two Army munitions that would be most heavily used in a conflict with China," said Mark Cancian, a retired Marine colonel and CSIS Defense and Security senior adviser. "You're not gonna use that many Javelins, for example, because the amount of ground combat is going to be relatively limited, even artillery will be limited, but air defense — missile defense — that will be huge." An April estimate from the Center for Strategic and International Studies showed that it currently takes defense contractors four years and five months to complete delivery of new THAAD interceptor contracts. Patriot PAC-3 interceptor orders have an average delivery time of three and a half years. CSIS' estimate said that before the Iran war, the U.S. entered 2026 with roughly 2,300 or so Patriot interceptors and expended between 1,050 and 1,430 during the conflict, potentially consuming as much as 61% of its prewar inventory. Fewer than 500 replenishment munitions were expected to be delivered in fiscal year 2026. The stockpile for THAAD systems prior to the Iran war sat at around 355 interceptors, with the Iran war using between 190 to 290, or about 82% of its prewar inventory, according to CSIS. There were no expected deliveries for replenishment in fiscal year 2026. In the current fiscal year — 2027 — the U.S. has requested more than 800 THAADs. Two of the nation's largest defense contractors — Lockheed Martin and RTX, through its Raytheon business — are involved in manufacturing these systems and their key components. They've recently signed agreements aimed at accelerating production. In January, Lockheed Martin announced a plan to quadruple the production capacity of THAADs from 96 to 400 interceptors per year. While the war with Iran has caused missile defense munitions to be depleted at a much higher rate, decades of Pentagon spending decisions, a shrinking defense industrial base and successive military operations that consume weapons faster than manufacturers can replace them have contributed to the current shortages. One U.S. official told CBS News that even if the United States could avoid expending additional THAAD or Patriot munitions in Iran or in other conflicts, it would take until the midterm elections of the next presidential administration — 2030 — to replenish the stockpile to the already-low December 2025 levels. Contacted by CBS News, Pentagon chief spokesman Sean Parnell said, "Claims of U.S. munitions shortages are false. When the Fake News media irresponsibly amplifies these lies, the real-world consequences is clear: our enemies are emboldened to provide — or attack — American troops." He added that the U.S. still has "everything required to strike at the time and place of the President's choosing." "Across multiple combatant commands," Parnell said, "we have already executed successful operations while maintaining a deep, ready arsenal to defend our people and our interests." How munitions are used around the world The U.S. military is divided into 11 unified combatant commands, each responsible for either a region of the world or specialized military mission. For operations against Iran, U.S. Central Command, led by Navy Adm. Brad Cooper, is in charge. Each combatant command needs a certain number of troops and weapons. The Pentagon uses a framework known as Global Force Management to decide where American troops, their units and some of the military's most sought-after weapons are sent around the world. The Global Force Management Allocation Plan, or GFMAP, is at the center of the process, laying out which forces will be provided to combatant commanders, for what missions and for how long. The plan is typically organized around the federal fiscal year. Generally, the Pentagon enters a new fiscal year with an existing plan for many of the forces expected to deploy or remain deployed during the coming 12 to 24 months, rather than deciding from scratch each time a commander asks for troops or weapons. But the plan is not set in stone. Wars erupt, crises develop, missions end and commanders are faced with unanticipated events to address. For instance, the commander of U.S. European Command might want more Patriots in Poland at the same time that U.S. Central Command wants those same resources in Kuwait, while U.S. Indo-Pacific Command may also need the systems for contingencies involving China. There's a constant shuffling of troops and assets from one region to another — in one instance in April 2025, Adm. Samuel Paparo, the commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, told the Senate Armed Services Committee that the Army had transferred a Patriot battalion from his region to U.S. Central Command amid ongoing fighting with the Iranian-back Houthi rebels in Yemen. What led to the current weapons systems shortage? After the collapse of the Soviet Union, American military planners abandoned the assumption that the U.S. might need to fight a prolonged war against another superpower, explained Cancian. "After the Cold War, we planned on fighting short regional conflicts against countries like Iraq or North Korea. And for those countries we didn't need the large inventories that we had needed during the Cold War," Cancian said. "We needed much smaller inventories." He added: "We shrank the industrial base. There was the famous 'Last Supper' which was literally a dinner that the deputy defense secretary put on for the heads of the defense industry, and he told them there's not enough money to keep you all in business, so you're going to have to consolidate or move out of the business, which they did." The resulting mergers reduced the number of major aerospace and defense contractors from 51 to five, according to the CSIS analysis. Also, historically, the Pentagon's procurement decisions have reduced spending on ammunition and missiles to free up money for fighter jets, tanks and warships, even while acknowledging that those weapons are essential to war fighting. Cancian told CBS News that the consolidation of the defense industrial base shaped an industry that produces efficiently during peacetime but is not designed to surge production. "We squeezed all the surge out because it was seen as unnecessary. So, that's where we end up when the war in Ukraine begins," said Cancian. "And after six months or so, we realized that we just don't have enough munitions and equipment for a protracted conflict." Under the Biden administration, there was a renewed interest in building surge capabilities back into the defense industrial base but that would take time. As the war between Russia and Ukraine began in full, the U.S. transferred roughly 600 Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine. However, not all of those weapons came from American military stockpiles; some were manufactured through the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative or provided by European countries. Additionally, both Biden and Trump administrations used Patriot and THAAD missile interceptors to defend Israel against Iranian strikes. Six months before Gen. George's warning assessment, U.S. forces fired roughly 150 THAAD interceptors and almost 80 Patriot interceptors during the Twelve Day War. Cancian noted that the five-year timeline to bring Patriot and THAAD stockpiles just to the low pre-Iran war levels is based on the assumption that the production schedule stays on track — and that additional military operations do not further deplete the inventory. President Donald Trump is making a broad assertion of executive privilege to keep secret the conversations he has had about plans to renovate the Kennedy Center, the Justice Department said in a court filing this week. A White House lawyer says in court documents released on Wednesday that Trump's executive privilege --which is the right of a president to keep confidential the communications he has with advisers -- would also cover his conversations with advisers who don't serve in government. Internal email points to Kennedy Center's continued closure The move comes as Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty, an ex officio trustee of the Kennedy Center, seeks to obtain information in her ongoing lawsuit challenging the planned closure and renovation of the performing arts center, and whether Trump has plans to demolish it. In a sworn declaration, Deputy White House Counsel Josh Hoyt said Trump’s executive privilege claim would cover any conversations the president has had with "his advisors (government and non-government)," including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Kennedy Center Executive Director Matt Floca, as well as anyone on his or the center's staff who may have advised Trump or his aides about "the President's duties and the effective functioning of the Kennedy Center." Mariam Zuhaib/AP - PHOTO: The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts is seen, Oct. 8, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Beyond the president's role as Kennedy Center board chairman, a position to which he was elected last year by his handpicked trustees, administration lawyers say, "in his capacity as President," Trump has "an official role in the Center’s operations." The Justice Department argues that since the law gives Trump the power to select who serves on the board, he must be positioned to assess whether current and future board members are "managing the Center ably and in accordance with their duties and statutory obligations." Kennedy Center Honors to be held at DC's Capital One Arena In a deposition taken earlier this month, an attorney who sat beside Floca repeatedly invoked executive privilege, rejecting questions from Beatty’s lawyer about the director's conversations with Trump, and even suggesting that queries about Floca’s talks with Lutnick could also violate Trump's privilege. Pushing back on the claims, Beatty’s lawyers have argued in court that "these blanket assertions of executive privilege are both procedurally and substantively improper." Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: Workers load in new barricades to be used in continuing to surround the main building of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C., Sept. 17, 2026. The Trump-aligned Kennedy Center board voted last month to close it for renovations after a federal judge's ruling blocked Trump's name from appearing on the outside of the building, a lawsuit Beatty initially brought last year. In May, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper issued an order blocking the planned two-year closure of the center for renovations, saying the board had not properly weighed the impact of the closure on the center’s finances and programming when it voted on the plan in March. The Justice Department later asked the judge to dissolve that order so planned renovations could proceed. Cooper has yet to rule on that motion. The suspect was shot and killed in the school by a member of the community who saw the suspect enter the building and pursued him, Krantz said. Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek praised the bystander for "heroically" intervening and stopping further loss of life. "Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well," Kotek said. A 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were also sent to a hospital with critical injuries. Krantz did not say what kind of gun the suspect used, although a law enforcement official briefed on the shooting told the Associated Press it was a pump-action shotgun. Police did not release the names of the victims or the shooter. What we know People stand near the scene of a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School on Oct. 15. via REUTERS / REUTERS Deschutes County dispatch received reports of an active shooter at 12:59 p.m. local time, from a person in a vehicle outside the school who said they had been shot at multiple times by someone with a long gun, according to Krantz . The suspect entered the school after shooting through locked doors. Law enforcement officers were alerted at 1 p.m. and the school went into lockdown at 1:01 p.m. Officers arrived at the scene at 1:02 p.m. and, moments later, an officer reported that a suspect had been shot by a community member. Federal law enforcement sources told Fox News the bystander had a concealed carry permit. "Our hearts are broken," said Bend Mayor Melanie Kebler during the press conference. "A school should be a safe place where children can learn and feel secure. What happened today should never happen." "We are stunned and heartbroken by this senseless tragedy," Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook wrote in a statement. "We extend our deepest sympathy to the families and to everyone affected by this violence. No words can adequately express the grief our community is experiencing. Our immediate priorities are caring for our students and staff and assisting law enforcement and emergency responders." FBI Director Kash Patel said the agency was on the scene assisting in the investigation. Bend-La Pine Schools said it had set up a family reunification site at a nearby church, and that all of its schools would be closed on Friday and any activities and athletic events would be canceled. "All Oregonians mourn this loss today," Kotek said. "This is a horrible day. No parent should have to have this kind of day and no community should have to live through this kind of day. We are going to do a lot of crying. We are going to cry together and we're probably going to cry privately." Police did not say if the shooter attended the school or knew any of the students. 'They're babies' Candles and flowers are seen at a makeshift memorial outside the Silver Rail Elementary School. PAYTON BRUNI via Getty Images Witnesses described hearing gunshots and seeing police swarm the school. "I heard what I thought was gunshots," Erin Johnson, who was visiting her parents next door to the school, told Oregon Public Broadcasting . "Then my neighbor began to scream shortly thereafter — her kids go to school there, at Silver Rail. Then I heard the police coming in. "It's heartbreaking. I don't know any details right now about who was injured. But they're babies." Krista Johnson told OregonLive she saw police swarm the school. "So many people stopping what they were doing," she said. "I knew that something had happened." Thousands attended a vigil at Bend's Drake Park on Thursday night, many carrying candles, flowers and stuffed toys, according to OregonLive. "There is power and love in this park tonight," Kotek said. "On behalf of everyone who lives in Oregon, I am so sorry for what you are experiencing today. No parent, no family, no community should have to have this kind of day." item.title: Body found in barrel at Lake Mead identified as 1980s shooting victim
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The remains of a man who was shot in the head and stuffed into a rusted barrel found on the shore of Lake Mead after the water level dropped were identified Thursday as an Arkansas man whose decades-old killing remains unsolved. Edward Lelburian Jackson was in his mid- to late 50s when he died, Clark County Coroner Melanie Rouse said. Authorities are looking for people to come forward to help solve Jackson's killing. There was no evidence directly linking the killing to organized crime in nearby Las Vegas despite longstanding speculation, although a connection hasn't been ruled out, police said. An expert on mob activity in the city said the case bears the "earmarks" of a mob hit and that questions still linger. The discovery sparked memories of Las Vegas' mob era Jackson was identified with the help of a bone sample sent for genealogy profiling, along with three angles of a composite face and clothing Jackson was wearing when he died, Rouse said. "We were able to confirm that the remains were in fact Edward Jackson," she said. The discovery of the barrel by boaters in May 2022 sparked memories of the city's mob era , which lasted from the 1940s to the mid-1980s. Organized crime helped build up Las Vegas, and a body stuffed in a barrel was known to signify a mob killing. Jackson, believed to be from Hot Springs, Arkansas, had a brief criminal history in the early 1980s in Salt Lake City, Utah, which included one charge of aggravated arson and conspiracy to commit fraud, said Robert Price, a Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department homicide lieutenant. Police said Jackson was married for a short time with no known children, CBS affiliate KLAS-TV reported . It's unclear why Jackson was in Las Vegas Price said there is nothing to tie the killing to organized crime. He added, however, that it hasn't been ruled out. Jackson's family told investigators that he liked to travel and detectives found records of him in California, where he lived with his wife in the early '70s. His family said they last saw him in Arkansas in the early '80s, and it is unclear why he was in Las Vegas. Homicide detectives will continue working to figure out what happened to him, said Price. "It's an unsolved case. It will never be closed until we solve it," Price said Thursday. "I would say that this is a piece of the puzzle and as we get more and more pieces, we'll be able to keep on digging deeper." Authorities had already said the man was shot, and they estimate he was killed in the early 1980s. Jackson had not been reported missing The man had been wearing a button-down short-sleeve shirt, light blue jeans, a silver wristwatch and blue-and-white tennis shoes. Price said the family didn't report him missing. "They knew that he had traveled the country, would show up when he showed up, just to say hi. But they didn't think anything other than that. They just figured he was out and about," he said. Researcher says case has all the "earmarks of a mob hit" Geoff Schumacher, vice president of research, collections and programs at The Mob Museum in Las Vegas, said there are still many questions about who Jackson was and what he was involved in that "earned him a trip in a barrel into the lake." Members of organized crime were involved in the Las Vegas casino industry from the 1940s to the mid-1980s, both behind the scenes and through shadow ownerships of casinos, Schumacher said. He said the case had all the "earmarks of a mob hit," mirroring another case from 1976 when Italian mobster John Roselli was killed and stuffed in a barrel and dumped into a bay outside of Miami Beach. Schumacher said he and Mob Museum staff will comb their records to try to help solve the case. "I think this story is not over," he said. Other bodies discovered as Lake Mead recedes Las Vegas historian Michael Green said whoever committed the crime probably thought the body would "never come near the surface." In the early 1980s, the lake levels were so high that the spillways flooded at Hoover Dam, he said. Now, Lake Mead is at a historic low due to years of overuse, longstanding drought and increasing temperatures. The water level of the 90-year-old reservoir has dropped, exposing areas that were previously underwater. In August, the water level dipped to 1,039.77 feet above sea level, according to the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation , well below the previous record low set in July 2022. Several other sets of remains were found at Lake Mead in 2022. Another set of skeletal remains was discovered that May, and they were identified as a drowning victim from 2002. Skeletal remains found in August were identified as a 52-year-old Las Vegas resident who disappeared in 1998. The remains of another drowning victim, Donald Smith, who was believed to have drowned in 1974 , were found in October 2022. Its receding waters are leaving behind the usual flotsam and jetsam of a lake heavily trafficked by weekend boaters — and even exposing a ship dating back to World War II. Lake Mead and the upstream Lake Powell are the largest human-made reservoirs in the U.S., part of a system that provides Colorado River water to people across the U.S. Southwest and Mexico. In 2022, Lake Mead's dropping level exposed Las Vegas' uppermost drinking water intake. That forced authorities to switch to a deeper intake to keep serving the city's 2.4 million residents. item.title: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia confirms she never passed bar exam
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia gave her first press briefing on Tuesday. But she has spent the days since then facing questions about her own legal credentials rather than President Trump's agenda. Trump announced last Friday that he had chosen Zacharia, a conservative commentator and former Department of Homeland Security spokesperson, to replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the administration in August. In his post on Truth Social announcing her appointment, Trump described Zacharia as an "attorney" as well as "a devoted fan and member of MAGA!" Zacharia holds both a law degree and a bachelor's degree from Pepperdine University, and her LinkedIn page says she served as "general counsel" at Fix California, a nonprofit founded by former acting Kennedy Center director Ric Grenell to promote conservative policies in the Golden State. In media appearances, she has described herself as a lawyer. But the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that while Zacharia sat for the California bar exam after graduating from law school, she "didn't pass." A senior administration official confirmed to NBC News that Zacharia did not pass the California bar exam. Reuters also investigated her credentials and "could not find records showing Zacharia was registered as an attorney or member of the bar in any U.S. state or the District of Columbia." Asked by reporters Tuesday on the South Lawn where she passed the bar, Zacharia twice replied, "When I moved to China." White House press secretary Katie Zacharia looks on as President Trump speaks to reporters on the South Lawn on Oct. 13. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson In a phone interview with the New York Times on Wednesday , Zacharia said she misheard the question. "I assumed the question was, 'Where were you after law school?'" she told the paper. "That's all I could hear over the sound of Marine One. And, wanting to respect protocol, the distance behind the president, kept me from moving closer to hear the question." Zacharia pointed out that it was only her second day on the job. In a statement to the Washington Post , the White House said that "Katie moved to China with her husband after graduating because of his job at an American private equity firm while she worked on international transaction law." According to USA Today , Zacharia "worked for a Chinese law firm's international-practice team on multimillion-dollar shareholder agreements involving investments through the World Bank." She did not attempt to take the bar exam a second time. On Thursday, Zacharia confimed that she did not pass the bar, telling the conservative outlet Real America's Voice that she was "incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited" at the time by her impending marriage and move to China. "We just said… 'I'll take the bar and see what happens,'" Zacharia recalled. "The results are somewhat inconsequential because I knew I wouldn't need the bar in China." Legal experts told the Times that it's debatable whether a law school graduate can describe herself as a "lawyer" before she passes the bar. But she cannot call herself an "attorney" — someone who is licensed to practice law and give legal advice — nor can she serve as a "general counsel" or as an "associate" at a Chinese law firm, they added. Zacharia told Real America's Voice that she was "very careful about how I executed this and I never came across as somebody who was an attorney-at-law." "I consulted for a very long time many people in the field — 'Is it OK and acceptable if I label myself 'lawyer' … and provide legal analysis, not legal advice," she explained. "They said, 'Absolutely,' across the board. 'You can call yourself a lawyer.'" On Wednesday, a nonprofit watchdog group called Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the California bar asking it to investigate whether Zacharia had violated state law by "repeatedly holding herself out as a lawyer." White House spokesperson Steven Cheung responded on social media by dismissing the Campaign for Accountability as a "radical leftist-organization run by rabid numbskulls suffering from a severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome." What happened in Zacharia's first briefing? White House press secretary Katie Zacharia speaks with reporters in the Briefing Room on Oct. 13. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson Zacharia's first briefing lasted 15 minutes, most of which was taken up by her opening statement. "I am so honored to work for President Trump and the American people as the new White House press secretary," Zacharia told reporters in the Briefing Room. "I want to thank President Trump for his trust that he has placed in me. I have wanted to work with him for a very long time." She took questions from three news outlets — Breitbart, Fox News and the Daily Mail — before ending the briefing. Asked what she planned to do as press secretary, Zacharia said, "I get to do what I was doing on the outside already, which was getting to amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump's incredible agenda for the American people." In his post on Truth Social announcing her appointment, Trump said Zacharia "has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning." Zacharia called the appointment "the honor of a lifetime" in a post on X . Who is Katie Zacharia? President Donald Trump and Katie Zacharia. Katie Zacharia/X The 42-year-old California native and mother of four left her role as senior communications adviser to Trump Media and Technology Group, which runs Truth Social, to join the White House. Before that, she served for about two months as a deputy assistant secretary and spokesperson for former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, according to her LinkedIn profile . She was best known for her frequent appearances defending the administration's policies on Fox News, CNN, Newsmax, One America News and other outlets. She told CNN in April — around the time she left DHS — that she's a "huge fan of ICE and a big fan of the Border Patrol." Zacharia first came to Washington in 2006 to intern for the Republican National Committee while George W. Bush was president. She lives in California with her husband and their four young children. During Tuesday's briefing, she was asked about juggling the competing roles of being a mother and White House press secretary. "The idea of not spending evenings with my kids is completely unacceptable," Zacharia said, before confusing her spouse with her boss. "So my president — excuse me, my husband — is out here." Zacharia then praised Trump as the "most family-friendly president we've ever had" and said her family will be moving from California to Washington, D.C., soon. CNN reported on Friday that Zacharia's "selection came about quickly" and that she "was not being considered for the role" as of "last week." CNN also reported that "on multiple occasions, senior officials had narrowed down the list" of possible press secretaries "only to find that candidates had said something negative about the president, disqualifying them from the position." In a New York Post column in February , Zacharia recounted a clash with liberal patrons of her "local cardio kickboxing gym" that ended with the gym owner asking her not to wear her red "Team Trump 2024" hat to exercise class. "I responded that I would never take my Trump hat off to appease the left," Zacharia wrote. "I refuse to stay silent." item.title: Fort Hood survivors praise Trump for scrapping execution livestream
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Survivors of the 2009 Fort Hood massacre praised President Donald Trump's decision not to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, after warning that broadcasting his death could turn the execution into a spectacle and hand terrorist groups a propaganda tool. Hasan is still set to be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3, 2026, and Trump said the immediate families of his victims will be permitted to witness the execution in person. But it will no longer be broadcast to the general public as previously announced by Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. Alonzo Lunsford, who was shot seven times by Hasan during the attack nearly 17 years ago, told Fox News Digital that Trump's decision is a "positive move." "It proves that we are a better people, a better nation, and that we're not barbaric," Lunsford said in immediate reaction to the walk-back by Trump on Thursday. "We don't glorify such actions." Veteran Shot 7 Times In Fort Hood Massacre Has A Warning For Americans Planning To Watch Execution Lunsford said he supports Hasan's death sentence and execution by firing squad but drew a line at broadcasting it to the public. Read On The Fox News App "For it to be made a spectacle for everyone to witness how they're gonna do a tailgate or, 'Hey, we're gonna have a cookout and we're gonna watch this man be put to death.' No, it's not about that," Lunsford said. "It's not a spectacle. It's not a pay-per-view event or a WWE wrestling match or even a boxing match." He also warned that footage of Hasan's execution could be seized upon by terrorist organizations. "You don't want that to be used as a tool for Isis or al-Qaeda to recruit and say, 'Hey, this is what happens to you if you do this against the infidel,'" Lunsford said. Julia Wilson was a civilian employee at Fort Hood when Hasan went on his rampage. She was nine months pregnant during the attack, which was carried out on her due date. Fort Hood Shooter Should Be Executed '13 Times Over' — But Not On Live Stream, Survivor Says She was slammed against a wall amid the chaos of the shooting and has said that it was only by the grace of God that she and her then-unborn son survived. Wilson was already against the livestreaming of Hasan's execution because she didn't want others to be traumatized like she was during the deadly attack. "I'm ecstatic about that," she told Fox News Digital, reacting to the news that the plan to livestream the event would not proceed. U.S. President Barack Obama (R) and first lady Michelle Obama pay their respects to the people killed as they attend a memorial service for the thirteen victims of the shooting rampage allegedly by U.S. Army Major Nidal Malik Hasan on November 10, 2009 in Fort Hood, Texas. Hasan, an army psychiatrist, is accused of killing 13 people and wounded 30 during a shooting at the military base. "I'm worried about other people's mental health," she continued. "I don't think the government… really put a lot of thought into how this was going to go down and how it was going to transpire until today." "I don't think they really thought about how this may affect people," said Wilson. "Seeing something like that affects your mental health. I don't care who you are. I don't care what you've seen. Seeing someone murdered in front of you or killed in front of you affects your mental health, whether they deserve it or not." Wilson also worried that if the livestream had proceeded, it would exist online forever, and that children might discover it while searching the web. "Once it's on out there, it's out there," she said. Trump said Wednesday that he believed publicly broadcasting Hasan's death could have served as a deterrent, but ultimately sided with those who opposed making the execution available for anyone to watch. "I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," Trump continued. "That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose. They deserve to witness JUSTICE!" Lunsford pointed to warnings surrounding Hasan before the shooting and criticized the Army's handling of the future attacker before he was transferred from Walter Reed to Fort Hood. "We knew this guy had issues," Lunsford said. "If you are privy to the ticking time bomb report, you will see what he was talking about. This guy had issues and they just passed the buck and moved him from Walter Reed to Fort Hood." Lunsford wondered what might have happened had Hasan deployed overseas before carrying out an attack. "Suppose he would have did the deed once he got in country on a FOB, a forward operating base," he said. "Imagine how many American lives would have been lost then." For Lunsford, allowing victims to witness Hasan's execution remains important even without a public broadcast. "It's gonna be a traumatic thing for, at least for the families of the fallen," he said. "They'll be able to close the chapter and hopefully close the book." "Every day we get up, we come to the VA hospital or we have to take our meds in the morning or we get ready to do something that we normally would have been doing prior to 5 November '09 that we're no longer able to do now, that's a constant reminder," he said. "I am no longer a victim of his," Lunsford added. "I'm a survivor."
